text:
I'm inclined to agree with the thin client notion others have expressed here, but in a somewhat different context. I foresee a long-term trend of virtualization in computing driven by the trend toward a Fourth Industrial Revolution accelerated by resilience imperatives compelled by climate impacts and the imperative to greater sustainability through the elimination of speculative production. And so I foresee the emergence of freely scalable, modular, dynamic gate array processing devices tracing their lineage back to Field Programmable Gate Arrays and the 'reconfigurable computing' based on them used for science applications and now being realized in so-called 'neuromorphic' and 'memristor' devices. Having properties of processors and memory together, the performance of these devices will be a function of array scales and the parallelism they allow rather than a competition of clock speeds. The premise behind the adoption of such devices will be the cultivation of supply chain resilience through increasingly ubiquitous and local production capability for these broadly multipurpose, lower tolerance, lower speed, lower power yet still high performance devices, eliminating the geographic and corporate production hegemonies of conventional microprocessors that will become an increasing liability as climate impacts worsen. The result will be a class of freely scalable computers with largely generic hardware and flexible architectures that exist in software. These, in turn, will increasingly merge functionality with communications hardware based on the same technology leading to a progressive merging of processing and communications infrastructure.
Put simply, we are looking at computers of much simpler, more generic hardware design using a smaller diversity of more multipurpose, ubiquitously produced, components as their architectures are virtualized as software. And with time these will increasingly become unseen parts of municipal communications infrastructure instead of sitting in homes and offices, except where certain facilities/users have some need for a high concentration of local processing power and storage under more independent management. Thus a trend in simpler mobile front-end user devices needing less on-board computing power and mass storage.
Along with this will develop P2P application platforms evolving from P2P/Decentralized web hosting and again motivated by resilience imperatives, the elimination of commercial client-server service hegemonies (with their increasingly plain pathological social influence), and the increasing community adoption of mesh-like telecommunications (with the decline of corporate telecom), leading to the realization of a virtual cloud computing environment where software and stored data exists online as encrypted entities independent of specific processing hardware distributed across peer networks managed on commons principles. In effect, the entire Internet will begin to function as a collective distributed virtual cloud computer spread across a global network commons of peer processing/storage nodes, increasingly embedded into the municipal telecom infrastructure and where user data environments, web sites, and applications exist as virtually indestructible (inadvertently) perpetually running software independent of any particular host computer.
Much more near-term, the dominant concern in computer hardware design will soon become adaptation to imminent plastics moratoriums and resource shortages with the use of alternative materials, the sustainability convention of Repair>Reuse>Repurpose>Recycle, and adaptations to localized independent production through Open Source technology and design as, again, compelled by resilience imperatives as well as part of a growing cultural backlash against corporatism and neoliberal economic exploitation through the emergence of a Global Swadeshi movement. There is an emergent class of goods whose designs are not owned or rather commons, intended for independent local production as a way to insure survival and living standards in times of emergency, but also as an antidote to the pathological dependencies --the ills of consumerism and colonialism-- fostered by the market economy's products. We are seeing people increasingly considering the underlying ethics of the products they choose and use as a function of how and where they are made as well as what they are made out of and how their use impacts society. And so some conscientious people are choosing simpler, lower-tech, less complex products with more open design on ethical grounds, questioning the quality-of-life gains and societal benefits forever promised by the pursuit of the cutting edge and forever new.
What this all means for computer design is more use of Open Source technology without exclusive component supply sources, a return to the 'PC clone' based on generic components and its expansion into the broader range of computing, electronics, and appliances, more use of materials like metal, wood, pressboard, and ceramics replacing plastics, and simpler, perhaps somewhat bulkier, designs favoring mechanical assembly intended to facilitate smaller scale lower-tech production, much easier repair, much easier recycling, and a greater basic durability for a longer use-life with greater return on resource investment. No more blobjects!
The Post-Industrial future is a place where most goods are made on-demand, near where you live if not in your own home, using designs globally distributed online, eliminating the wastes of speculative production and the long-distance transport of elaborately packaged bulky fragile finished goods. To facilitate this paradigm, most goods will need to be redesigned to accommodate this mode of production and the factoring out of production methods needing excessive facility scales, heavily polluting industrial processes, and vast pools of capital investment. And society itself will need to become more industrially and agriculturally literate, ending the pathology of social Taylorism and the dependencies it fosters. More people will need to know how to make, grow, and repair more things for themselves and their neighbors. This is not too difficult for most goods defining our standard-of-living which are, already, predominantly produced in job shops rather than the old fashioned factories of the past. But it will be more of a challenge for electronics and computing products with sophisticated production processes and where engineering knowledge must be encoded into the topologies of modular component standards to reduce skill in production and service. (as was the key virtue of the PC design and reason for its revolutionary rate of adoption and improvement)
But the disruptions of climate impacts and delayed adaptation may also bring some unusual design trends due to limited availability of certain components. Flat panel displays are particularly subject to geographic supply hegemonies and may be resistant to production localization. And so supply chain disruptions caused by climate impacts may create chronic shortages for these now crucial components, compelling development of more easily fabricated alternatives. This is particularly problematic for mobile devices and we could see more reliance on e-ink displays or the emergence of a new class of sound/voice based mobile computers as a result, as their hardware would be much cheaper and easier to produce everywhere. Basically, mobile computers reduced to displayless hands-free devices the size of the old iPod with a Bluetooth headset and perhaps a subvocal speech collar as a user interface. This could lead to the advent of hands-free computing and a kind of digital telepathy where instant messaging is replaced by 'party lines' of silent subvocal conversation.
